item.title: The Happiness Myth Almost Everyone Believes
item.description:
Happiness

The Happiness Myth Almost Everyone Believes

What 80 years of research says actually predicts a happy life.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Strong relationships predict happiness better than money or achievement.
  • Helping others can boost your happiness, purpose, and sense of connection.
  • Lasting happiness often grows through connection, not constant self-improvement.
  • If you want to feel happier, invest in people, not just yourself.

Complete this sentence. “I would be happy if I only had a little more....”

If you’re like most people, you’d probably say “Money” or something similar to “rock-solid abs.” Most of us have a running list in our heads of things that must change in our lives before we can be happy. We often assume happiness is waiting just beyond the next achievement.

However, the evidence suggests that money only accounts for about 2 percent of the variance in happiness between people. And dieting can actually end up hurting happiness.

Maybe focusing on the numbers on the scale or in your bank account is not the way to get happier. If those pursuits don’t move the needle nearly as much as we’d expect, then where does happiness actually come from?

Science suggests that if you want to be happy, the key may be to start turning your attention away from yourself and toward others.

Research shows us, again and again, that the most relevant ingredient for happiness is feeling socially connected. For example, the longest-running study of human happiness (spanning across three generations and 80 years), the Harvard Longitudinal Study, found that high-quality relationships were the single most important factor for happiness throughout the lifespan. After decades of tracking careers, wealth, health, and relationships, researchers reached their remarkably simple conclusion. The quality of our relationships predicts happiness better than anything else studied.

Another study found that those who set and worked toward social (aka relatedness) goals reported greater gains in happiness than those who worked on personal growth goals. Rather than trying so hard to change yourself, if you really want to be happier, you might try putting that effort toward your relationships.

Beyond social connection, contributing to others’ lives is a potent way to become happier. Many studies have shown that altruism not only benefits the receiver but the giver as well. Doing things for others releases dopamine (and in fact, trait altruism is related to the specific D4 dopamine receptor) and feels good. Helping others literally activates the brain’s reward system, and it shows. People who do more good deeds for others report higher life satisfaction, greater positive affect, and lesser negative affect.

In a 2019 study, participants were asked to either do a good deed for others (e.g., donate to charity, give a compliment, etc.) or to practice some form of self-care (e.g., eating a nice meal, taking oneself out to a movie, etc.). After 10 days, their changes in happiness were tracked. While both groups experienced increases in well-being on days when they completed either task, the participants who did good deeds for others reported feeling more socially connected and a greater sense of purpose.

Taking care of yourself is important. As the saying goes, you have to put your own oxygen mask on first. But when taking care of your happiness, don’t forget about social connection and altruism as important parts of your self-care routine. Call up an old friend to catch up, and savor the joy you feel when laughing with them. Or help a stranger with their groceries. It’s ok if you’re only doing it for the free dopamine—no one has to know.

item.title: 5 Ways to Cope When You Don’t Have Family Support
item.description:
Family Dynamics

5 Ways to Cope When You Don’t Have Family Support

Estrangement can leave you without family to lean on. Build your own safety net.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Estrangement often means facing life's hardest moments without family to fall back on.
  • Missing that support isn't weakness; it's the real cost of losing people you counted on.
  • You can build your own support system, deliberately, from friends, community, and the people who show up.

The form at the doctor’s office asks for your emergency contact, and you sit there, pen hovering over the line, not sure whose name to write. It’s a small moment. But if you’re estranged from your family, you know these are the moments where the loss lives.

Some days, the feelings hit hard: grief, anger, and the ache of missing what’s gone. But estrangement costs you more than the relationship. It quietly strips away everything that person was supposed to provide. The ride home after surgery. Someone to show up when you’re sick, or overwhelmed, or scared. The person who has known you your whole life and would pick up the phone at 2 a.m.

When family is the thing you’ve had to step away from, or the thing that stepped away from you, you don’t just lose the people. You lose the safety net that came with them.

I’ve worked with estranged people for over a decade, and I’ve lived this myself. So I want to say clearly: the hurt you feel isn’t weakness, and it isn’t a sign you made the wrong choice.

What Estrangement Takes From You

Estrangement leaves a real absence behind, and it shows up in more than one form. There’s the practical support: the concrete help most people don’t think twice about, because they’ve always had it. And there’s the emotional support: the sense that someone in the world is in your corner by default, no explaining required.

Some people lose family support to death, and they’re dealing with a lot of the same things you are. But estrangement carries something bereavement usually doesn’t. The person may still be alive, the relationship is unresolved, and the loss often goes unrecognized by the people around you. There’s no funeral for a family you’ve cut contact with, and grief without that kind of closure carries its own particular burden.

Estrangement also rarely stays contained to one person. When a relationship ruptures, unfortunately, people often take sides. The other parent, siblings, aunts, and uncles line up behind someone else, and you can find yourself without them too. One rupture can empty out a whole side of a family.

When There Are No Grandparents to Call

Parenting without family support is harder than most people realize. You watch other people hand their kids to grandparents for the weekend, lean on relatives for the school pickup, call their mom when the baby won’t stop crying. You have none of that, and the exhaustion of doing it all alone is real.

Sometimes what’s missing isn’t just the help, but the map. A father teaching his son to throw a ball, when no one ever taught him, is doing something he was never shown how to do.

It’s normal to feel a flash of envy at that built-in support, and the pressure of doing it all yourself. Naming that isn’t self-pity; it’s accurate. You’re carrying a genuine load, not falling short of some standard everyone else meets easily. And often, you’re doing it so your children inherit something different from what you did.

How to Build Your Own Safety Net

While it’s true that estrangement can leave you without a support system, you can build one that catches you when you fall. Here’s where to start.

1. Notice when you’re doing it all alone. If no one showed up for you growing up, you often learn to need no one. You become fiercely independent, the person who handles everything solo. John Bowlby called this compulsive self-reliance, and while it kept you safe once, it can quietly keep you isolated now. Try catching the moments you reach for “I’ve got it” when you don’t have to. Then, every so often, let someone help anyway.

2. Let people in, a little at a time. For a lot of estranged adults, trusting people is genuinely hard. You might manage friendly, surface-level relationships but find that letting anyone truly close feels almost impossible. If that sounds like you, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not the only one. But your hurt happened with people, and so does the healing. You don’t have to trust everyone, or all at once. Just let one safe person a little closer than feels comfortable, and see what happens.

3. Find others who get it. There’s real comfort in being around other people who are estranged. No explaining, no defending your choices. That’s what estrangement support groups and online communities are for, and being understood without having to make your case is its own kind of relief.

4. Create your own support system. When you can’t count on the family you were born into, you build one of your own. Friends, a partner, a neighbor, a community or faith group, a therapist. Ask yourself: if something went wrong tonight, who would I turn to? If you can’t answer easily, that’s not a failure. That’s just where it starts.

5. Solve the practical gaps before the crisis. Some of the hardest times sneak up on you: who checks in when you’re sick, where you spend the holidays, who you’d even ask for help in a pinch. Think them through while things are calm, so you’re not scrambling when they aren’t. Line up a couple of people you can lean on.

You Shouldn’t Have To, and You Can

I’m not going to tell you any of this is fair, because it isn’t. You shouldn’t have to build a support system from scratch when others are simply handed one. But I’ve watched people do it, and the safety net you build is no less real for having been chosen.

So, if you don’t yet have anyone to write on that emergency contact line, it doesn’t mean you’re alone forever. It just means there’s a name you haven’t met yet, or one you haven’t thought to ask.

item.title: The Sex Problem Isn't About Sex
item.description:
Sex

The Sex Problem Isn't About Sex

Vulnerability, empathy, intimacy, and emotional investment strengthen desire.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual conflict often reflects deeper relationship dynamics rather than problems with sex itself.
  • Vulnerability, empathy, intimacy, and investment create an emotional foundation for lasting sexual connection.
  • Accountability helps partners recognize how each contributes to emotional distance.
  • Repair becomes possible when couples rebuild connection instead of focusing only on symptoms.
Source: peopleimages12/123rf

Love: A Relationship Built on Passion and Connection

Maya and Connor used to describe themselves as best friends and passionate lovers. Early in their relationship, they talked easily, laughed often, and felt deeply connected. Physical affection came naturally. Sex was never something they negotiated or worried about; it was simply one expression of the closeness they shared.

Over the years, life became more complicated. Their careers became more demanding, they welcomed two young children, and their responsibilities multiplied. Like many parents, they found themselves spending more time caring for their children than nurturing their relationship.

Even so, they remained deeply committed to one another and to their family. From the outside, they appeared to be doing well. Inside the relationship, however, they felt increasingly disconnected. The affection, playfulness, and unhurried conversations that once came naturally gradually gave way to packed schedules, responsibilities, and exhaustion.

Crash: When Sex Becomes the Focal Point

Neither Maya nor Connor could remember exactly when the arguments began. They only knew that nearly every disagreement eventually circled back to the same subject: sex.

Months passed without physical intimacy. When Connor initiated sex and Maya declined, he experienced it as rejection and feared she no longer desired him. Maya experienced the situation very differently. Exhausted, sleep-deprived, and overwhelmed by parenting, she saw sex as one more demand at the end of an already impossible day. Her priority was getting enough sleep to function.

The more Connor raised the subject, the more pressure Maya felt. The more pressure Maya experienced, the more Connor interpreted her withdrawal as rejection. Each responded to the other’s behavior without fully understanding the feelings underneath it.

Eventually, the same argument repeated itself in different forms. Connor believed Maya was no longer making their relationship a priority. Maya felt Connor had reduced their relationship to whether or not they were having sex. Neither could understand the other’s perspective.

The more they fought, the more emotionally distant they became. Eventually, even mentioning sex triggered another argument. What neither initially recognized was that their conflict was no longer just about sex. It was also about loneliness, exhaustion, rejection, resentment, misunderstanding, and emotional disconnection.

Maya gradually stopped sharing her most vulnerable thoughts because she feared criticism, disappointment, or another painful conversation. Connor also became emotionally guarded. Beneath his frustration were loneliness, insecurity, and a growing fear that he was no longer wanted. Their conversations became increasingly transactional, affection became less frequent, and emotional distance gradually replaced emotional closeness.

In Love. Crash. Rebuild., we describe four foundational pillars that support healthy relationships: vulnerability, empathy, intimacy, and emotional investment. As those pillars weakened, Maya and Connor became increasingly focused on the symptom—the absence of sex—while overlooking the deeper relational issues beneath it.

Sexual intimacy often flourishes when emotional intimacy has a strong foundation. When vulnerability, empathy, intimacy, and emotional investment begin to weaken, sexual desire often weakens with them.

Rebuild: Using PACER to Restore the Four Pillars

Pause

The turning point came when they stopped asking, “Why aren’t we having sex?” and began asking a different question: “What has happened to us?”

Pause helped them step back from the recurring argument and examine the deeper pattern beneath it. They realized they were no longer talking about sex as an expression of love, connection, and intimacy. Instead, conversations about sex had become conversations about loneliness, rejection, pressure, resentment, and exhaustion. The problem suddenly looked much larger—and much deeper—than either had realized.

Accountability

Connor acknowledged that he often approached the issue through frustration rather than vulnerability. Instead of admitting he felt lonely, insecure, or unwanted, he expressed anger, criticism, and blame. Maya acknowledged that she had gradually withdrawn emotionally and physically from the relationship. Rather than sharing how overwhelmed, exhausted, and emotionally depleted she felt, she often avoided the conversation altogether.

Neither partner intended to hurt the other. Both had been trying to protect themselves from emotional pain while unintentionally creating more distance.

Collaboration

As they talked more openly, they began exploring what sex actually meant to each of them. For Connor, sexual intimacy represented emotional connection, reassurance, and feeling desired by his partner. For Maya, emotional closeness was a prerequisite for sexual intimacy. She needed to feel emotionally safe, accepted, and connected long before she could desire physical intimacy.

For the first time, they stopped arguing about frequency and began discussing meaning. They realized they weren’t simply disagreeing about sex—they were approaching intimacy through different emotional pathways. Instead of debating who was right, they began asking what each needed to feel connected.

Experiment

Rather than focusing immediately on rebuilding their sex life, they focused on rebuilding the four pillars.

  • They practiced greater vulnerability by sharing fears and insecurities they had previously kept hidden.
  • They strengthened empathy by listening to understand each other’s experience rather than preparing a defense.
  • They intentionally created opportunities for intimacy through conversation, affection, humor, and quality time.
  • They increased their emotional investment by treating their relationship as something that required ongoing care rather than something that could survive on autopilot.

These changes did not create an overnight transformation. Instead, they gradually rebuilt something even more important than sexual frequency: a stronger emotional foundation.

Reset

Over time, the emotional atmosphere of the relationship began to change. Conversations became more open, honest, and compassionate. Affection returned naturally, and both partners increasingly felt understood, appreciated, and emotionally connected.

Sex also returned—not because either partner forced it, negotiated it, or won an argument, but because they intentionally rebuilt the emotional conditions that allowed intimacy to grow again. They also recognized that raising young children required them to be intentional about creating opportunities for intimacy rather than waiting for spontaneity. Instead of viewing planned intimacy as less romantic, they learned to see it as another way of investing in their relationship.

Their goal was no longer simply to have more sex. It was to build a relationship where both emotional and physical intimacy could thrive.

Why This Matters

Couples often focus on sexual problems because they are highly visible, emotionally charged, and difficult to ignore. Yet many conflicts about sex are rooted in deeper relationship dynamics.

When vulnerability, empathy, intimacy, and emotional investment begin to weaken, sexual desire often weakens as well. The absence of sexual intimacy is not always the primary problem. Sometimes it is one of the clearest signals that the relationship itself needs attention.

The PACER process helps couples move beyond symptoms and explore the deeper dynamics beneath them. Sometimes the sex problem isn’t actually about sex. It’s about rebuilding the emotional foundation that allows intimacy to thrive.

item.title: Emotionally Healthy Dating After Divorce or Separation
item.description:
Mating

Emotionally Healthy Dating After Divorce or Separation

Advice to wait a year before dating is not empirically supported.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • No evidence supports waiting one year to date after divorce; emotional readiness matters more than time.
  • Healthy dating starts with self-awareness, accountability, and emotional regulation—not loneliness or revenge.
  • Emotionally mature relationships support healing, identity growth, and long-term well-being after divorce.
Source: Jep Gambardella / Pexels

Common advice that family and friends give recently separated or divorced people is to give themselves a year before jumping back into the dating scene. There doesn’t appear to be any empirical evidence to support the recommendation.

A better indication of your psychological readiness to date again starts with the motivation to date in the first place. Here are a few questions you can ask yourself to clarify motivation:

1. Am I dating to validate my attractiveness or ability to attract dates?

2. Am I dating because I’m lonely and/or depressed?

3. Do I fear being alone?

4. Am I angry at my ex-partner or spouse and want them to know I’m dating someone new so as to exact revenge or inflict emotional pain of some kind?

Psychological readiness to date can be understood as being in a state of approaching desired experiences that do no harm, versus avoiding discomfort or wishing to make an ex uncomfortable.

As Langlais and Frye-Cox (2026) found in a recent study of mothers’ post-divorce dating transitions, most periods of adjustment in and out of a romantic relationship are associated with stress and short dips in well-being. Being uncomfortable at the start of and end of a relationship is normal.

Even emotionally healthy relationships will bring a set of stressors as two adults navigate the inevitable differences that come with intimacy, including different interests, lifestyles, and roles (especially for those with children).

The psychologically ready dater is not one without a mental health history, previous relational challenges, or, as stated earlier, someone who has quarantined themselves from romance for a prescribed time period.

Beyond ideal motivations, it is someone who has adequate emotional intelligence and reflective functioning. An emotionally mature adult has both the capacity to introspect and a track record of effective emotional regulation before and after separation.

They have spent the requisite time meaningfully answering the question: How did I contribute to the relationship issues I faced in my past serious romantic partnership or marriage? Even in the most asymmetrical toxic relationships, one can consider the variables that contributed to their partner selection or the red flags purposefully ignored. More likely, post-divorce or separation can illuminate relationship skills deficits including clear communication, seeking understanding, emotional validation, and boundary setting or reinforcement.

Without this self-reflective functioning, no amount of time post-divorce or separation will suffice to ready someone to date again. Daters beware: there are likely many on the dating apps and lurking at your local pub who have not done the work and don’t even know how to do it. They may lack the emotional intelligence to see that there is work to be done in the first place. They may also be one of the notorious covert narcissists who has blamed the dissolution of every relationship they’ve had on their partner, taking no accountability in a rare form of self-protection that keeps them blind to their own dysfunction.

The good news is that emotionally healthy dating is possible, regardless of your previous marital status or relationship history. In fact, there’s longitudinal evidence that dating an emotionally mature person who’s able to create a high-quality relationship with you has lots of benefits: buffering stress and providing emotional, social, and practical support. This can be a particularly wonderful turn of events for a single parent who integrates a romantic partner into their family life in later stages of a dating relationship when there has been significant consistency, dependability, and commitment.

Lastly, one of the most important elements of post-divorce dating is that it extends identity reconstruction beyond what’s possible individually. For people who have been in only one long-term relationship previously, getting new, real-time interpersonal feedback from an emotionally safe partner can solidify newly explored facets of identity and reinforce stable characteristics that promote self-esteem.
